title: Word Break

scenarios.scenario: Text segmentation in languages without spaces
scenarios.description: Breaking compound words or continuous text (like in Chinese or Japanese) into meaningful dictionary words for translation or processing.
Determining if a domain name or URL can be decomposed into valid registered subdomains or recognized patterns.
Validating if a variable name or identifier can be broken down into meaningful dictionary words, useful for code analysis and naming convention checks.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.approach: Use recursive backtracking to try matching each word in the dictionary at the current position. If a word matches, recursively check if the remaining substring can be segmented. Return true if we reach the end of the string.
solutions.explanation: The recursive solution explores all possible ways to segment the string. Starting from index i, we try each word in wordDict. If a word matches the substring starting at i, we recursively check if the rest of the string (starting from i + len(word)) can be segmented. The base case is when i equals the length of s, meaning we've successfully segmented the entire string. If any recursive path returns true, we've found a valid segmentation. This approach systematically tries all possibilities but may recompute the same subproblems multiple times.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution works by exploring all possible ways to segment the string using words from the dictionary. At each position i, we try to match every word from the dictionary. If a word matches (checked by substring comparison), we recursively verify if the remaining portion of the string can be segmented. The base case ensures that we've consumed the entire string, meaning all parts matched dictionary words. If any path through the recursion tree reaches the base case, we've found a valid segmentation. The correctness relies on exhaustive search - we try all possibilities until we find one that works or exhaust all options.
common_mistakes: Not checking if i + len(w) exceeds the string length before substring comparison, causing index errors.
Using s[i:i+len(w)] == w without bounds checking, which can create incorrect substrings.
Forgetting the base case i == len(s), leading to infinite recursion or incorrect results.
Returning true immediately when finding a matching word without checking if the rest can be segmented.
pro_tips: The substring comparison s[i:i+len(w)] == w is O(t) where t is the word length, contributing to overall time complexity.
This recursive solution has overlapping subproblems - the same index i is visited multiple times through different paths, making it a candidate for memoization.
The condition (i + len(w)) <= len(s) prevents array out of bounds errors.
Understanding this brute force approach is essential before optimizing with DP.

solutions.title: Recursion (Hash Set)
solutions.approach: Convert wordDict to a hash set for O(1) lookup. Instead of iterating through dictionary words, iterate through all possible ending positions and check if the substring is in the set. This allows more flexible exploration of segmentation points.
solutions.explanation: This optimization converts the word dictionary to a hash set for constant-time lookup. Instead of trying each word and checking if it matches, we iterate through all possible ending positions j from the current position i. For each position, we extract the substring s[i:j+1] and check if it exists in the word set. If it does, we recursively check if the rest of the string can be segmented. This approach is more flexible than the first solution as it doesn't require iterating through the potentially large wordDict for each position. However, without memoization, it still suffers from exponential time complexity due to overlapping subproblems.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution works by systematically trying all possible split points in the string. At each position i, we consider all substrings starting at i and check if they exist in the dictionary (using O(1) hash set lookup). If a substring is valid, we recursively verify that the remaining portion can be segmented. The hash set optimization makes the word lookup faster than iterating through wordDict. The base case ensures we've consumed the entire string. While this approach is more elegant than iterating through the word list, it still explores all possible segmentations without caching results, leading to repeated computation of the same subproblems.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Top-Down)
solutions.approach: Add memoization to the recursive solution to avoid recomputing the same subproblems. Store whether each index can lead to a valid segmentation in a memo dictionary. This transforms the exponential solution into polynomial time.
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes the first recursive approach by adding memoization. We use a dictionary memo where memo[i] stores whether the substring starting at index i can be segmented into dictionary words. Before computing dfs(i), we check if we've already solved it by looking in memo. If found, we return the cached result immediately. Otherwise, we compute it using the same logic as the recursive solution: try each word from wordDict, and if it matches at position i, recursively check the rest. We store the result in memo before returning. The base case memo[len(s)] = True is initialized upfront. This eliminates redundant computations by ensuring each index is solved exactly once.

complexity_explanation.space: The memo dictionary stores boolean results for at most n indices, requiring O(n) space. The recursion stack can also be O(n) deep in the worst case. Total space is O(n).

solutions.why_it_works: Memoization eliminates the exponential time complexity by caching results for each index. The key observation is that whether we can segment the string starting from index i depends only on i, not on how we reached i. This means we have overlapping subproblems - the same index i might be reached through different segmentation paths. By storing the result for each index the first time we compute it, all subsequent calls with the same index can retrieve the cached value in O(1) time. This transforms the problem from exploring all 2^n possible segmentations to solving n independent subproblems, each of which tries m words. The correctness is preserved from the recursive solution while achieving polynomial time complexity.

Storing only successful results (True) but not failures (False), leading to recomputation of failed paths.
Checking memo after trying all words instead of before, missing the optimization.
pro_tips: Top-down DP with memoization is often easier to implement than bottom-up because it follows the natural recursive structure.
Initializing memo with the base case {len(s): True} simplifies the recursive function.
This pattern of adding memoization to recursion is widely applicable - identify overlapping subproblems first.
In interviews, starting with recursion and then adding memoization shows clear problem-solving progression.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Hash Set)
solutions.approach: Combine hash set optimization with memoization. Convert wordDict to a set and find the maximum word length. Use memoization while iterating through possible ending positions, but limit the search to the maximum word length to avoid unnecessary checks.
solutions.explanation: This solution combines the best of both worlds: hash set for O(1) word lookup and memoization for avoiding repeated computation, plus an optimization to limit the search range. We first convert wordDict to a set and compute the maximum word length t. For each index i, instead of checking all positions from i to len(s), we only check up to min(len(s), i+t), since no word can be longer than t. We use memoization to cache whether each index can lead to valid segmentation. This reduces unnecessary substring operations and lookups for very long strings. The combination of these optimizations makes this one of the most efficient solutions.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution optimizes both the word lookup and the search range. Using a hash set makes word lookup O(1) instead of O(m). Limiting the search to the maximum word length avoids creating and checking substrings that are too long to match any dictionary word. Memoization ensures each index is computed once. The combination of these optimizations significantly reduces the practical runtime. The correctness is preserved: we still check all valid segmentation possibilities (substrings up to max word length), but skip impossible ones (substrings longer than any word). This makes the solution efficient even for long strings with short dictionary words.

Forgetting that the base case i == len(s) must be checked after memo lookup to avoid missing the cache.
Not understanding that the optimization only helps when t << n (max word length much smaller than string length).
pro_tips: The max word length optimization is most effective when the dictionary contains short words and the string is long.
This solution demonstrates how multiple optimizations can be combined: hash set (O(1) lookup), memoization (avoid recomputation), and pruning (limit search space).
The loop range min(len(s), i+t) ensures we don't go beyond the string length even if i+t exceeds it.
This is one of the most practical solutions for real-world applications where dictionaries often have bounded word lengths.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up)
solutions.approach: Build the solution iteratively from the end of the string to the beginning. Use a boolean array dp where dp[i] represents whether the substring starting at index i can be segmented. For each position, try all dictionary words and update dp[i] based on whether the word matches and dp[i+len(word)] is true.
solutions.explanation: The bottom-up approach eliminates recursion by building the solution iteratively. We create a boolean array dp of size n+1, where dp[i] indicates whether the substring s[i:] can be segmented into dictionary words. We initialize dp[n] = True (empty string is valid). Then we iterate backward from n-1 to 0. For each position i, we try every word in the dictionary. If a word matches at position i and dp[i+len(word)] is True (meaning the rest can be segmented), we set dp[i] = True and break (no need to try more words). This iterative approach computes the same values as top-down DP but in reverse order without recursion. The answer is dp[0].

complexity_explanation.time: We iterate through n positions backward. For each position, we try all m words from the dictionary. For each word, we do a substring comparison which takes O(t) time where t is the word length. The early break optimization helps in practice but doesn't change worst-case complexity. Total time is O(n*m*t).
complexity_explanation.space: We use a dp array of size n+1, requiring O(n) space. No recursion stack is needed, making this more space-efficient in practice than top-down DP.

solutions.why_it_works: Bottom-up DP works by building solutions to larger problems from solutions to smaller problems. The recurrence relation is: dp[i] = True if there exists a word w such that s[i:i+len(w)] == w and dp[i+len(w)] == True. By iterating backward from n-1 to 0, we ensure that when we compute dp[i], all values dp[i+1], dp[i+2], ..., dp[n] have already been computed. The base case dp[n] = True represents that an empty substring can always be segmented (vacuously true). This approach avoids recursion entirely, making it more efficient in practice due to eliminating function call overhead. The early break when dp[i] becomes True is an optimization that skips checking remaining words once we've found one valid segmentation.

constraints_examples.explanation: Build dp backward: dp[8]=T, dp[4]=T (from 'code'), dp[0]=T (from 'leet'). Return True.
No position can set dp[i]=True leading back to dp[0]=False.

common_mistakes: Iterating forward instead of backward, which causes you to access dp[i+len(w)] before it's computed.
Forgetting to initialize dp[len(s)] = True before the loop.
Using dp[i] = True instead of dp[i] = dp[i+len(w)], which ignores whether the rest can be segmented.
Not breaking early when dp[i] becomes True, leading to unnecessary word checks.
Off-by-one errors in array indexing or loop bounds.
pro_tips: Bottom-up DP is generally more efficient than top-down in practice because it avoids recursion overhead.
The early break optimization significantly improves performance when multiple words match at a position.
The iteration order (backward) is critical - we must compute smaller subproblems (larger indices) before larger subproblems (smaller indices).
This solution is optimal in both time and space complexity and is often preferred in interviews for its clarity.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Trie)
solutions.approach: Use a Trie data structure to store the dictionary words for efficient prefix matching. Build a DP array bottom-up, but instead of checking each word individually or using hash set lookups, use the Trie to check if substrings are valid words. This optimizes the word lookup especially when there are many words with common prefixes.
solutions.explanation: This advanced solution uses a Trie (prefix tree) for efficient word lookup. We first build a Trie containing all dictionary words. Each node in the Trie has children (character mappings) and a boolean flag indicating if it's the end of a word. We then use bottom-up DP similar to solution 5, but instead of iterating through all words, we iterate through possible ending positions (limited by max word length) and use the Trie's search method to check if s[i:j+1] is a valid word. The Trie allows us to quickly check word membership with early termination if a prefix doesn't exist. This is particularly efficient when the dictionary has many words with common prefixes.

complexity_explanation.time: Building the Trie takes O(m*t) time where m is the number of words and t is average word length. Finding max word length takes O(m). For the DP, we iterate through n positions, and for each position, we check at most t ending positions. Each Trie search takes O(t) time to traverse the Trie. Total time is O(m*t) for Trie construction + O(n*t*t) for DP = O((n*t^2)+m).
complexity_explanation.space: The Trie stores m words with average length t, requiring O(m*t) space in the worst case (no shared prefixes). The dp array requires O(n) space. Total space is O(n+(m*t)).

solutions.why_it_works: The Trie provides efficient word lookup with early termination for invalid prefixes. When searching for s[i:j+1] in the Trie, if we encounter a character that doesn't exist in the current node's children, we can immediately return false without checking the rest. This is more efficient than substring comparison when there are many words with common prefixes. The DP logic is the same as solution 5, but we use Trie.search instead of iterating through all words or using hash set lookup. The Trie's structure naturally encodes prefix relationships, making it ideal for string matching problems. The max word length optimization limits the search range, preventing unnecessary long substring checks.

common_mistakes: Not initializing TrieNode.children as an empty dictionary/map in the constructor.
Forgetting to set is_word = True at the end of insert, making all words unfindable.
Off-by-one errors in Trie search range (should be idx <= j, not idx < j).
Not handling the loop range correctly in the DP iteration (should include i = len(s)).
Assuming Trie search is always faster - for small dictionaries, hash set can be more efficient.
pro_tips: Tries are most beneficial when the dictionary has many words with common prefixes, as they share storage.
The Trie search method could be optimized to return early if we've already determined dp[i] = True.
This solution demonstrates an advanced data structure application, showing depth of algorithmic knowledge.
In practice, hash set solutions (solution 4) are often simpler and sufficient unless the dictionary is very large with many shared prefixes.
The Trie can be extended to solve Word Break II (finding all segmentations) more efficiently.

notes: This is a classic DP problem demonstrating string segmentation. The key insight is that segmentability at position i depends on finding a word starting at i and the segmentability of the remaining string. Multiple optimization techniques can be applied: hash set for fast lookup, max word length pruning, early break, and Trie for prefix-based matching. Solutions 3, 4, and 5 are most practical, with solution 4 offering the best balance of efficiency and simplicity. The Trie solution is more advanced and beneficial for large dictionaries with shared prefixes.
